opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that MCTS is basically a way of converting compute at inference time into playing strength. You have a policy network that gives you a prior over moves, and a value network that tells you roughly how good a position is, and search lets you refine both of those by actually looking ahead and checking whether your intuitions hold up.

Empirically, what you see is that playing strength goes up roughly with the log of the number of simulations. So going from, say, 100 to 1,000 simulations gives you a big jump, and going from 1,000 to 10,000 gives you another jump that's maybe comparable in Elo, but you're paying ten times more compute for it. It's this diminishing-returns curve, and it looks a lot like the scaling laws people talk about for pretraining, just on the inference side.

The interesting subtlety is that the curve depends a lot on how good your network is. If your policy and value networks are weak, search helps enormously, because it's correcting a lot of mistakes. If your network is very strong, the raw policy with zero search is already playing at a high level, and each additional simulation is mostly confirming what the network already believed. There's a trade-off between training compute and test-time compute: you can get to a given strength with a bigger, better-trained network and less search, or a smaller network and more search.

There's another piece too. In AlphaZero-style training, search is the policy improvement operator. The network gets trained to imitate what MCTS found, so more simulations during self-play give you better targets. But there's a sweet spot, because if you spend all your compute on deep search per move, you generate fewer games and your data throughput drops. Getting that balance right was one of the things I found most interesting to tinker with.

And I think that's why this matters beyond board games. The lesson that you can trade inference compute for capability, with a fairly predictable log-linear relationship, is exactly what people are now seeing with reasoning models in language. Board games were a clean sandbox where you could see that relationship very clearly.

r001.rationale: The response says the strength curve depends on network quality and that search helps more when the policy and value networks are weak.

r002.rationale: It states that playing strength goes up roughly with the log of the number of simulations and describes gains as simulations increase.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the number of simulations is basically a knob on how much compute you're spending at test time, and playing strength scales with that, but it's a pretty specific kind of scaling. The classic plots from the AlphaGo and AlphaZero papers show Elo going up roughly linearly in the log of the number of simulations. So you double your search budget and you get some fixed bump in Elo, and then you double it again and you get about the same bump. It's diminishing returns in absolute terms, but it's remarkably consistent over many orders of magnitude.

What I find interesting is what that curve is actually telling you about the policy and value networks. If you run zero simulations, you're just sampling from the raw policy prior, and that's your floor. That floor is already quite strong for AlphaZero because the policy has been distilled from millions of search results during training. Search then acts as a policy improvement operator on top of it. Every simulation is correcting for places where the prior is wrong or where the value estimate is noisy. So the slope of that Elo-versus-log-simulations line is a measure of how much headroom there is between what the network already knows and what the network plus deliberation can figure out.

The other thing I'd point out is that the relationship isn't fixed across training. Early in training the network is bad, so search gives you a huge relative boost because it's doing most of the work. Late in training the network has absorbed a lot of what search was discovering, and you need more simulations to get the same marginal gain. There's this amortization loop where test-time compute gets converted into weights, and then the weights raise the baseline for the next round of search. That's really the core idea of AlphaZero and it's the same idea people are now excited about with language models and reasoning, just with a different search procedure.

And then there's the practical caveat, which is that MCTS relies on a good simulator and a discrete action space. In Go you can spend a thousand simulations because the environment is perfect and cheap. In robotics, which is where I spend most of my time, you don't have that. Your model of the world is imperfect, so more simulations just means more rollouts in a slightly wrong model, and at some point the compounding error dominates and more search actually makes you worse. So I'd say the clean log-linear relationship is a property of domains where the simulator is trustworthy, and figuring out how to get something like it when the simulator is learned is one of the big open problems.

r001.rationale: The response says the search benefit changes with network strength: weak networks get a large boost, while stronger networks need more simulations for the same marginal gain.

r002.rationale: It describes strength rising with simulation count in trustworthy-simulator domains, but says additional search can make performance worse when the simulator is imperfect, so it does not establish a general monotonic increase.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that MCTS lets you trade computation at decision time for playing strength. You have a policy that gives you an initial guess about promising moves, and a value function that estimates how good a position is. Search lets you refine those guesses by exploring what happens next.

Generally, more simulations make you stronger, but with diminishing returns. Going from ten simulations to a hundred can make a big difference; adding ninety simulations when you’re already doing a million probably won’t. And the relationship depends on how good the underlying policy and value function are. A stronger model can direct its search toward useful branches, so each simulation accomplishes more.

There’s also a limit to what search can fix. If your value function systematically misjudges a position, you can spend a lot of computation reinforcing that mistake. So simulation count alone isn’t a universal measure of strength. It’s the interaction between the learned model and the computation you give it.

r001.rationale: It says the relationship depends on the underlying policy and value function, and that a stronger model can make each simulation more useful.

r002.rationale: It says more simulations generally make play stronger, but does not state that strength increases monotonically; it also notes that more computation can reinforce a mistaken evaluation.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that the policy network gives you an initial intuition about which moves are good, and MCTS lets you spend more computation checking that intuition. As you increase the number of simulations, you generally get stronger play, but with diminishing returns. Going from one simulation to a hundred is a much bigger deal than going from a million to a million and a hundred.

And the relationship depends on the network you’re searching with. A stronger policy directs search toward promising moves, and a stronger value function helps you evaluate the positions you reach. So a simulation isn’t a fixed unit of playing strength. You can improve by doing more search, or by improving the model that makes that search useful.

That’s what makes this interesting as a model for reasoning: you can take the same trained network and get better decisions by giving it more time to think. But how effectively it uses that extra time depends on what it learned during training.

r001.rationale: The response says the strength gained from simulations depends on the network used for search, including its policy and value functions.

r002.rationale: It says that increasing simulations generally produces stronger play, while gains diminish as the count grows.
